messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: QA Engineer
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Media / News: Related news
  Maladaptive Strategies: Counterfactual Thinking: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred, Avoid Police: Police, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo is a 24-year-old QA engineer who lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment in a sprawling suburban complex outside a major city. He came to therapy reluctantly, nudged by his supervisor after a series of missed deadlines and a tense exchange with a coworker who had innocently mentioned a news segment about a recent subway derailment. For Mateo, that word—derailment—was not a piece of information. It was a door that swung open and pulled him back into a Thursday evening eleven months ago, when his own life came off its tracks.

The disaster had been man-made—a signaling system failure that caused a packed commuter train to slam into an oncoming freight on a curve. Mateo had been riding in the third car, returning from a client meeting. He remembered the lurch, the screaming, the acrid smell of burning metal and the sight of a woman pinned beside him, her leg bent at an impossible angle. He had tried to help, but he was dazed and blood was streaming down his own face. By the time emergency workers arrived, the woman was unconscious. Mateo survived with a concussion and a deep gash on his arm, but something inside him had splintered. In the weeks that followed, he learned that the crash was caused by a software bug in the train's control system—the exact kind of flaw he spent his days trying to catch before release. The thought hollowed him out. He should have seen it. He should have done something. Others died; he did not, and he was certain that failure to protect them would follow him forever.

In the months after the crash, Mateo's world contracted. He stopped watching any news at all, not just about the accident but about everything, because he never knew when a headline might mention a collision or a recall or a safety violation. He unfollowed social media accounts that posted current events, and when a friend started talking about a documentary on infrastructure failures, Mateo excused himself to the bathroom and stayed there until the friend left. The hardest avoidance came during his commute. He could not bring himself to ride the subway again, so he drove—a forty-five-minute trip each way through congested highways that left him exhausted. But driving was tolerable because he was in control. What he could not stand was the feeling of going numb, of the world tilting into unreality, that crept up on him when he stood in a crowded station or heard the screech of train brakes. That dissociative sensation terrified him more than any memory, because it made him feel as though he were not entirely here, as though the crash had never fully ended.

His work suffered. As a QA engineer, he was expected to run tests, write reports, and collaborate on safety reviews. But every mention of a "critical failure" or "edge case" at team meetings made his chest tighten. He began to avoid certain coworkers who had a habit of swapping stories about past bugs that had caused real-world damage—what he called "crash discussions." He asked to be moved to a different project, claiming he needed a change, but really he was trying to steer clear of any conversation that could steer toward accidents. His supervisor noticed his withdrawal and his plummeting productivity; the missed deadlines piled up. In the performance review, Mateo said nothing about the crash. He was ashamed. He was also convinced that nothing good could happen to him anymore. Every small setback felt like confirmation that his life had reached its ceiling.

He had come to believe that the world was full of hidden dangers, and that anyone—a colleague, a stranger, a train operator—could be the unwitting agent of harm. He scanned faces in parking lots, checked door locks twice, and distrusted the intentions of people he had no reason to fear. Police officers made him uneasy, not because he had ever been in trouble, but because they were the ones who had taken his statement at the hospital, their questions implying he might have missed something. He avoided them now, crossing the street if he saw a squad car. His social life evaporated. Friends stopped inviting him out because he always said no, and he spent his evenings replaying the moments before the impact, wondering what he could have done differently—if he had stood in a different spot, if he had warned someone, if he had never taken that train at all.

By the time his supervisor sat him down with a list of resources, Mateo was sleeping poorly, eating erratically, and feeling as though he was simply waiting for the next bad thing. He came to the first session with his arms crossed, reluctant, but also carrying a thin thread of hope—that maybe, somewhere beneath the rubble of his old self, something might still be salvageable.
